words_to_read_new.meaning: in- means in + STRUCT means build: to build knowledge into someone, to teach
con- means together + STRUCT means build: to build together
STRUCT means build + -ure means the result of: the result of building, something built
in- means in + STRUCT means build + -or means one who: one who builds knowledge into you
in- means in + STRUCT means build + -ion means the act of: the act of building knowledge in
con- means together + STRUCT means build + -ion means the act of: the act of building together
de- means opposite of + STRUCT means build + -ion means the act of: the act of tearing down what was built
re- means again + con- means together + STRUCT means build: to build together again
ob- means against + STRUCT means build: to build something against the way through, to block

sessions.wtr_new_notes:
SAY: "Learn struct once and you can read a whole family of words about building."
READ each word as it appears, say what it means, then link struct to the card meaning: build.
instruct - in means in + STRUCT means build: to build knowledge into someone. The coach will instruct us on the rules.
construct - con means together + STRUCT means build: to build together. Workers construct a bridge piece by piece.
structure - STRUCT means build + ure means the result of: something built. The climbing frame is a steel structure.
instructor - in + STRUCT + or means one who: the one who builds knowledge into you. My swimming instructor.
instruction - in + STRUCT + ion means the act of: the act of building knowledge in. Read every instruction first.
construction - con + STRUCT + ion: the act of building together. The construction of our new gym took a year.
destruction - de means opposite of + STRUCT + ion: the opposite of building, tearing down. The storm left a trail of destruction.
reconstruct - re means again + con means together + STRUCT means build: to build together again after a fire or flood.
obstruct - ob means against + STRUCT means build: to build something against the way through. A fallen tree can obstruct a road.

keyword_sentence.title: Pick your own struct word
keyword_sentence.rule: Two jobs in your OG book
keyword_sentence.example:
1. Your own struct word for build. Star it.
2. Write one sentence that shows what it means.
items: My word: **construct** - Dad will **construct** a new cubby.
keyword_sentence.footer: Check: does it make the meaning clear?
keyword_sentence.notes:
1. SAY: "The card keyword is construct. Con means together, struct means build. You can see every part, so it is a strong keyword."
2. SAY: "If another struct word helps YOU remember build, pick that one. Write it at the bottom of the page and star it."
3. SAY: "Then write one sentence with your word, so a reader can tell what it means." TIME: 3 min, then cold call two students to read theirs.
EXTENSION: Two in one - write one sentence that uses two struct words and still makes sense.
HELP: give a stem, "The workers will construct..." or "Our coach will instruct...", and let them finish it.
---
ANSWERS: open - e.g. Mine: construct. Dad will construct a new cubby. EXTENSION: e.g. The instructor showed us how to construct a raft.

matrix.title: Build struct words
matrix.rule: Build real words. Write each one and what it means.
matrix.notes:
1. SAY: "struct is in the middle. Join a part from the left, the right, or both, and build a real word. Write the word and what it means."
2. MODEL: say "con plus struct: construct, to build together", and write it on the class board.
3. TIME: 4 min. CIRCULATE: to a stuck student say, "Start with struct. Put in in front. What does instruct mean?"
4. ASK: "Read me your longest word and what it means." Cold call two students. EXPECT: reconstruction, the act of building together again; constructive, relating to building.
TRAP: a made-up word that sounds right, like destructure. Fix: ask, would you read that in a newspaper? Student builds a real one.
EXTENSION: Longest word hunt - build the longest real word you can and write its parts.
HELP: give three starters, construct, instruct, obstruct, and ask for one ending on each.
---
ANSWERS: construct, instruct, obstruct, destruct (as in self-destruct), reconstruct; add -ion: construction, instruction, obstruction, destruction.
Also: constructor, instructor (one who); constructive, instructive, destructive (relating to); structure; constructed, obstructed.
EXTENSION: e.g. reconstruction = re + con + struct + ion.

intro.title: Noun, verb or adjective?
intro.rule: Read the sentence. What job does the bold word do?
intro.prompt: The **construction** of our new gym took all year.
intro.why: construction is the thing that took all year
intro.footer: Next: your turn on four suffix cards
intro.notes:
ANSWER: noun - construction is the thing that took all year.
1. SAY: "Last week you voted noun, verb or adjective the trickiest, so we practise it again. The sentence tells us the job."
2. POINT at each choice. SAY: "A noun names a thing or idea. A verb is something you do. An adjective describes a noun."
3. MODEL: read the sentence. SAY: "What took all year? The construction. It is the thing in this sentence."
4. SAY: "The doing word here is took. Construction does not describe anything. So it is a noun." REVEAL on the click.
5. SAY: "Construct is something you do. Add -ion, the act of, and it becomes a thing. The suffix changed the job."
TRAP: verb, because construct is an action. Fix: cover the -ion, then show it; student says what the suffix changed.

cards.sentence: The accountant counted the school's money.
cards.why: accountant is the person doing the counting
cards.notes:
1. READ: "Read the card with me." CHORAL: "-ant means one who or that which. The accountant counted the school's money."
2. ASK: "What job does accountant do in this sentence: noun, verb or adjective?"
10 sec, turn and talk. Then: "Everyone, together, on three."
EXPECT: noun.
SCAN: split or wrong chorus -> do not click. Ask "Who did the counting?", then re-ask on three.
3. REVEAL after the choral answer. SAY: "The accountant is the person doing the counting, so it is a noun. -ant often names a person who does something, so those -ant words are nouns."
TRAP: verb, because counted is an action. Fix: counted is the verb; ask who counted, student points at accountant.

cards.sentence: The new library has an angular roof.
cards.notes:

2. ASK: "What job does angular do in this sentence: noun, verb or adjective?"
10 sec, turn and talk. Then: "Everyone, together, on three."
EXPECT: adjective.
SCAN: split or wrong chorus -> do not click. Ask "What sort of roof is it?", then re-ask on three.
3. REVEAL after the choral answer. SAY: "Angular describes the roof, so it is an adjective. -ar means relating to, so -ar words often describe."
TRAP: noun, because roof is a thing. Fix: roof is the noun; ask what sort of roof, student says angular.

10 sec, turn and talk. Then: "Everyone, together, on three."
EXPECT: noun.
SCAN: split or wrong chorus -> do not click. Ask "What runs every ten minutes?", then re-ask on three.
3. REVEAL after the choral answer. SAY: "Service is the thing that runs every ten minutes, so it is a noun. -ice words name a state or a thing, so they are nouns."
TRAP: verb, because you can service a car. Fix: read the sentence - here nothing is being serviced; ask what runs, student says service.

grammar.header_notes:
PURPOSE: However and therefore tell the reader how two full sentences connect. A semicolon goes before them and a comma after.
WHY THIS WEEK: in Week 3 we used however and therefore as connectives; last week the semicolon joined two full sentences. Today they work together.
TIME: 5 minutes, no more - I do 1 min, We do 1 question, You do 3 questions at about 30 seconds each. One question per slide; your click reveals the answer.
ROUTINE: all grammar is written in the OG book. No boards - books, fingers and voices only.
CHECK: semicolon before, comma after, and each side must make sense as a full sentence on its own.

i_do.title: Join with however or therefore
i_do.rule: Semicolon, then however or therefore, then a comma.
i_do.example:
We built a cubby; however, the roof leaked.
It rained all day; therefore, we stayed in.
items: however = the other side, a surprise
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: We built a cubby; however, the roof leaked.
1. SAY: "However and therefore tell your reader how two ideas connect. However shows the other side. Therefore means so, the result."
2. WRITE: copy "We built a cubby. The roof leaked." on the class board. CROSS OUT the first full stop. WRITE a semicolon, however and a comma, and change The to a small t. However takes a small h too.
3. ASK: "Is a leaking roof a surprise, or the result of building? Thumbs up surprise, thumbs down result, voices off." 5 sec. EXPECT: thumbs up, so however.
4. POINT at the second example. SAY: "Staying in is the result of the rain, so therefore."
TRAP: a comma before however. Fix: a comma cannot join two full sentences; student swaps it for a semicolon.
CLARIFY: if asked why not just but or so, say however and therefore make a persuasive piece sound grown-up, and when they join two sentences into one, they need the semicolon.
---
PREP: semicolon + however or therefore + comma is still one sentence, so the word after the comma takes a small letter.

we_do.title: However or therefore?
we_do.rule: Pick the word that shows how the ideas connect.

round.prompt:
Our team trained all winter; ___,
we won the grand final.
round.why: winning is the result of training
round.notes:
ANSWER: 2 - therefore. Winning is the result of all that training.
1. SAY: "Read it in your head. Is winning a surprise, or the result?"
2. ASK: "One finger however, two therefore, three and, voices off, show me on three." 5 sec. EXPECT: two fingers.
3. REVEAL after fingers are scanned. ASK: "How do you know?" Cold call one student. EXPECT: they won because they trained.
TRAP: choosing 3. Fix: after the semicolon this gap needs however or therefore, then the comma; student votes again.
CLARIFY: if a student says however, ask "Would winning surprise us after all that training?" No, so therefore.

you_do.title: Write the joining words
you_do.rule: Write the semicolon, however or therefore, and the comma.

round.prompt:
We packed our raincoats ___
we stayed dry on the hike.
round.answer: We packed our raincoats; therefore, we stayed dry on the hike.
round.notes:
ANSWER: ; therefore, - We packed our raincoats; therefore, we stayed dry on the hike.
1. SAY: "Write only the joining words: the semicolon, however or therefore, and the comma. Pens down when you are done."
2. TIME: 30 sec. SCAN four books near you. 80%+ -> click to reveal. Less -> ask "surprise or result?", then re-ask.
3. REVEAL after books are scanned. SAY: "Tick it or fix it. Staying dry is the result of the raincoats, so therefore."
TRAP: a capital T on Therefore, like in Week 3. Fix: after a semicolon it is still one sentence; student writes a small t.
EXTENSION: Two in one - write one sentence with a semicolon and however that uses two struct words.
HELP: write ; ______ , in their book so they choose only the word.

round.prompt:
The builders worked all weekend ___
the hall was still not finished.
round.answer: The builders worked all weekend; however, the hall was still not finished.
round.why: a surprise after all that work
round.notes:
ANSWER: ; however, - The builders worked all weekend; however, the hall was still not finished.
1. SAY: "Write the joining words. Pens down when you are done."
2. TIME: 30 sec. SCAN four books near you. 80%+ -> click to reveal. Less -> ask what we expected after a whole weekend of work, then re-ask.
3. REVEAL after books are scanned. SAY: "Tick it or fix it. We expected a finished hall, so not finished is the other side: however."
TRAP: therefore. Fix: the work did not cause the hall to be unfinished - it is a surprise; student swaps to however.

round.prompt:
The plan for the new structure was great ___
the council rejected it.
round.answer: The plan for the new structure was great; however, the council rejected it.
round.notes:
ANSWER: ; however, - The plan for the new structure was great; however, the council rejected it.
1. SAY: "Last one. Write the joining words. Pens down when you are done."
2. TIME: 30 sec. SCAN four books near you. 80%+ -> click to reveal. Less -> ask whether a great plan usually gets thrown back, then re-ask.
3. REVEAL after books are scanned. SAY: "Tick it or fix it. A great plan that gets rejected is a surprise, so however."
4. SAY: "In your next persuasive piece, use however to show the other side, and therefore to show a result."
TRAP: a capital T on the. Fix: still one sentence; student writes a small t.
---
ANSWERS: 1. ; therefore,  2. ; however,  3. ; however,
EXTENSION: e.g. The council wanted to construct a pool; however, the old structure was in the way.

vote.title: Trickiest this week?
vote.rule: Which was trickiest this week? Hold up 1, 2, 3 or 4.
vote.notes:
1. SAY: "Before we finish, I want to know what was trickiest this week. Read the four choices with me."
2. ASK: "Hold up 1, 2, 3 or 4 fingers for the trickiest one, voices off, show me on three." 5 sec. Count the most common number.
3. WRITE the winner into next week's From our reviews line.
